segments.narration: In 27 BCE, one of the two giant stone statues suddenly started singing every morning. Tourists sailed down the Nile just to catch the eerie chime echoing across the desert dawn.
A massive earthquake had just shattered the northern statue, cracking it from waist to crown. Ever since the rubble settled, the wounded giant greeted the sunrise with a clear, haunting note.
For centuries, the sound baffled everyone who heard it. Was it a trapped spirit? Roman emperors carved Latin poetry into the boots to honor the musical god.
Then, a Roman emperor tried to fix the damage. In 199 CE, workers stacked new sandstone blocks to patch the fractured torso, accidentally silencing the desert forever.

The morning sun heating moisture inside the cracked, porous stone had been the source all along. The repair work altered the temperature, permanently turning off the world's most famous acoustic illusion.

accuracy_flags.claim: Two giant stone pharaohs started singing every morning in ancient Egypt.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference states it was one statue (the northern colossus) that made the sound, not both pharaohs, and it was not every single morning consistently (though frequently reported around dawn).

verdicts.claim: An earthquake cracked the northern Colossus of Memnon in 27 BCE.
verdicts.note: The reference states that in 27 BCE, a large earthquake reportedly shattered the northern colossus, collapsing it from the waist up and cracking the lower half.

verdicts.claim: Roman emperors and poets traveled to hear the mysterious dawn sounds.
verdicts.note: The reference mentions that visitors included several Roman emperors, and Julia Balbilla recorded visits in poetry.

verdicts.claim: Roman Emperor Septimius Severus ordered the statue repaired in 199 CE.
verdicts.note: The reference notes local tradition places the reconstruction circa 199 and attributes it to Emperor Septimius Severus.

verdicts.claim: The repairs permanently silenced the stone voice by changing its temperature dynamics.
verdicts.note: The reference mentions the sound ceased, probably due to the added weight of the reconstructed upper tiers, and that natural explanations involved rising temperatures and the evaporation of dew inside the porous rock.
